questions.statement: The book ___ I borrowed from the library is overdue.
questions.context: A relative clause attached to the previous noun.

options.feedback: Correct! The pronoun refers to the book and stands in the subject position inside the clause.
It has no antecedent of its own, because the book is already the subject of the main clause.
This is a demonstrative and cannot introduce a relative clause.
One is an indefinite pronoun and cannot introduce a relative clause either.

questions.explanation:
A relative pronoun refers back to the noun in front of it. That is the safest choice when the noun is a thing and the pronoun is the clause subject.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The film ___ we saw was directed by a woman from Chile.
questions.context: The word that must be used because the antecedent is the object.

options.feedback: Correct! The pronoun is the object of saw, and that is the correct object form for a thing.
What is only used when there is no antecedent, and the film is the antecedent here.
Which is possible in formal English but that is the more usual everyday object pronoun.
Where replaces a place preposition, and there is no place in this clause.

questions.explanation:
A relative pronoun that stands for a thing can be who, which, whom or that, but in the object position that is the standard everyday form.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The year ___ she graduated is 2019.
questions.context: The question word that replaces a pronoun plus preposition.

options.feedback: Correct! When replaces the phrase in which and the clause then has its own subject she and verb graduated.
That cannot replace a preposition, and the clause has no verb that it could be the subject of.
Which would need the preposition at the end, such as which she graduated in, which is clumsy.
What cannot be used with a noun antecedent like the year.

questions.explanation:
Relative adverbs replace the pronoun plus the preposition. In which becomes when, on which becomes where, and for which becomes why.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: That is the colleague ___ I asked for help with the project.
questions.context: The possessive relative pronoun.

options.feedback: Correct! The clause refers back to the colleague with a preposition, so the subject is the relative pronoun itself.
Who would be the subject of the clause, but the clause has no verb after it.
Which cannot refer to a person, and the antecedent is a colleague.
That would also be a subject, but whose is the standard form when the preposition is the final element.

questions.explanation:
When a relative clause ends in a preposition, the relative pronoun becomes the object of that preposition. The antecedent and the preposition decide which form is right.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: ___ the tickets ___ for the evening show?
questions.context: A passive question, which needs the be auxiliary.

options.feedback: Correct! A passive question takes the auxiliary before the subject and the participle after.
Did builds active questions, and the tickets cannot book themselves.
That is the active form, and in the active the subject would have to be the one doing the booking.
A continuous would suggest the tickets are doing the booking, and the sentence is a simple question.

questions.explanation:
A passive question keeps the same structure as a passive statement with the auxiliary moved to the front: have the tickets been booked.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The photographs ___ by the photographer were published in the newspaper.
questions.context: A reduced relative clause with a past participle.

options.feedback: Correct! A reduced passive relative clause keeps the participle and drops the relative pronoun and the auxiliary.
A reduced clause drops the relative pronoun, so the two words together would be incorrect.
A reduced clause has no auxiliary, because that work is done by the main verb of the sentence.
Taking is the -ing form, and it would reduce an active clause rather than a passive one.

questions.explanation:
A reduced relative clause never keeps the auxiliary. The photographs that were taken becomes the photographs taken, and the meaning stays passive.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: When we ___ the results tomorrow, we will celebrate.
questions.context: A future sentence where the time clause keeps the present simple.

options.feedback: Correct! A future time clause takes the present simple, and the future sits in the main clause.
This is the classic error: a future form inside a clause that refers to the future.
The past simple would refer to a past moment, and tomorrow is still ahead.
A present continuous would be possible for a fixed arrangement, but the general rule here is the present simple.

questions.explanation:
English keeps the if, when and before clauses in the present tense when they refer to the future. Only the main clause carries the future tense.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I need to ___ the electrician ___ the wiring.
questions.context: The causative structure, with a to infinitive after get.

options.feedback: Correct! Get plus object plus to infinitive is the standard causative structure.
With get the infinitive keeps its to, so the base form without to is wrong here.
Make plus object takes a bare infinitive, so the to would be incorrect.
Got is the past of get, and the sentence is about something still to be arranged.

questions.explanation:
Get somebody to do and have somebody do are the two common causatives. The difference is the to: get keeps it and have drops it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: If I had known the answer, I ___ it to you yesterday.
questions.context: The third conditional with a mixed result.

options.feedback: Correct! A past perfect condition with would have plus participle gives the third conditional.
A would without have would place the telling in the present, and yesterday is in the past.
A past perfect in the result would reverse the two events, putting the telling before the knowing.
A future form cannot belong to a conditional about two past events.

questions.explanation:
The third conditional is made of two past forms. The if clause takes had plus participle and the result clause takes would have plus participle.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The students ___ in the library are preparing for the exam.
questions.context: A reduced relative clause with an -ing form.

options.feedback: Correct! An active reduced relative clause uses the -ing form and drops the relative pronoun and the auxiliary.
A reduced clause drops the relative pronoun, so that cannot remain in front of the participle.
A reduced clause has no auxiliary, because the main verb of the sentence carries the tense.
A bare base form is not the form of a reduced relative clause.

questions.explanation:
An active relative clause reduces to the -ing form, while a passive one reduces to the past participle. Neither keeps the auxiliary or the relative pronoun.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "The bridge ___ last month," the guide said. The guide said the bridge ___ last month.
questions.context: A passive reported statement where the auxiliary shifts.

options.feedback: Correct! A past simple passive backshifts to the past perfect passive.
Keeping the same tense would leave the two past events unordered, and the reporting verb is past.

options.text: has been repaired ... had been repaired
options.feedback: The first tense does not match the original past simple, so the report is not accurate.
A present passive in the second clause would break the backshift that the past reporting verb requires.

questions.explanation:
Backshift in a passive sentence changes only the first auxiliary. Was repaired becomes had been repaired, and the rest of the phrase is untouched.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The form ___ yet, so you will have to complete a new one.
questions.context: A present perfect passive with a singular subject.

options.feedback: Correct! A singular subject takes has plus not plus been plus participle.
Did cannot carry a perfect structure and would be active in any case.
A past passive would close the action in a finished past moment, and yet keeps the period open.
That is the active form, and the form cannot submit itself.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect passive reports a present state. Not having submitted anything is the reason a new form is needed now.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Where are you going?" she asked. She asked where I ___.
questions.context: A reported question with backshift.

options.feedback: Correct! The present continuous backshifts to the past continuous, and the word order becomes that of a statement.
Keeping the present would require a present reporting verb, and she asked is in the past.
A present perfect would place the journey in the present period, and the question is about a plan.
The past simple would backshift a past simple, and the original is a continuous form.

questions.explanation:
A reported wh question keeps its question word and loses the question word order. The tense backshifts by one step as it does in a statement.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The evidence ___ by the police was later dismissed.
questions.context: A reduced relative clause in a formal text, with a passive participle.

options.feedback: Correct! A passive reduced clause keeps the past participle and the by phrase retains the agent.
Collecting is the -ing form, which reduces an active clause rather than a passive one.
A reduced clause drops the relative pronoun, so that cannot stay in the phrase.
A reduced clause has no auxiliary, since the main verb of the sentence already carries the tense.

questions.explanation:
Formal and academic writing uses reduced relative clauses constantly. The evidence collected reads as a single noun phrase with the by phrase attached.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "Did you see the play?" she asked. She asked whether I ___ the play.
questions.context: A question about a past event in reported speech.

options.feedback: Correct! The past simple backshifts to the past perfect in reported speech.
Keeping the past simple would leave the two events without a fixed order.
A present perfect would be right with a present reporting verb, but she asked is in the past.
A past continuous would suggest the seeing was under way, which the original question does not.

questions.explanation:
A reported polar question keeps the tense of its clause and only changes the word order. Backshift applies to the tense just as it does in statements.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The application ___ before Friday, so please hurry.
questions.context: A modal in a passive, in the present.

options.feedback: Correct! Modal plus be plus participle builds a passive, and the deadline makes it an obligation.
That is the active form, and it would put you in the subject position.
The main verb after be must be a past participle, and submit is the base form.
Being belongs to continuous passives, and this is a modal passive.

questions.explanation:
A modal passive always places the modal before be and the participle after it. The order modal, be, participle never changes with the tense.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I wish I ___ more free time to practise the guitar.
questions.context: A wish about the present, with a negative.

options.feedback: Correct! Wish about a present situation takes the simple past in the that clause, and had not is the negative form.
A present form would state a fact, and wish needs an unreal situation.
A future perfect would place the free time in a possible future, which is not what the wish is about.
Had had would express a wish about a past situation, and the practice is a present concern.

questions.explanation:
Wish plus had expresses an unreal present, and inserting not gives the negative form. The structure is identical to the past one, with only the time of the situation differing.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: "My brother, ___ is an engineer, lives abroad," she said. She said that her brother, ___ was an engineer, lived abroad.
questions.context: A relative clause with a non-defining comma, reported in the past.

options.feedback: Correct! A non-defining clause with a past reporting verb backshifts the past simple to the past perfect.
Lives would require a present reporting verb, and she said is in the past.
Which cannot refer to a person, and the antecedent is her brother.
That is not used in a non-defining clause after a comma, because that would restrict the noun.

questions.explanation:
A non-defining clause adds extra information and takes a comma. It uses who, whom, whose or which, but never that, and the tense backshifts like any other clause.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Having ___ the report, the secretary left the office early.
questions.context: A sentence with a reduced relative clause and a participle phrase.

options.feedback: Correct! A perfect participle phrase at the start of a sentence takes the past participle and expresses an action completed first.
The -ing form would express an action in progress, not one completed before the leaving.
A base form cannot appear after having, which requires a participle.
A past participle after having would need the verb to be passive, and the secretary is the one finishing.

questions.explanation:
A perfect participle phrase begins with having plus past participle and shows that the first action happened before the main verb.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The office ___ every night, so the building is always empty in the morning.
questions.context: A causative combined with a passive structure.

options.feedback: Correct! A routine service described with an unspecified doer takes the present simple passive.
The active would make the office the one doing the cleaning, which is not what happens.
A past passive would place the cleaning in a finished past moment, and the habit continues.
A continuous would describe a single action under way, and every night describes a habit.

questions.explanation: A sentence about a service arranged by somebody is naturally passive. The doer is left out because the point of the sentence is the work done, not who did it.
questions.subject: ingles
